analytic.title: TRACES: Proactive Safety Auditing for Multi-Turn LLM Agents via Trajectory-State Modeling

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: LLM agents increasingly operate through multiturn tool use and environment interaction, where safety risks often emerge from intermediate steps long before they surface in the final outcome. Reactive auditing is therefore insufficient: post-hoc diagnosis frequently misses the chance to flag risks while they are unfolding. We propose TRACES, a representationbased proactive auditor that learns prefix-level trajectory risk states from the hidden representations of an observer LLM. TRACES induces latent mechanism features from step representations and models their temporal evolution to estimate whether a partial trajectory is drifting toward unsafe behavior. To sidestep the cost and ambiguity of step-level risk annotation, TRACES is trained with weak trajectorylevel supervision while still producing dense prefix-level risk estimates. Across multiple agent safety benchmarks, TRACES improves both full-trajectory safety prediction and proactive risk discrimination. Our analyses further suggest that these risk states can help train a safer agent, highlighting the broader potential of proactive auditing for long-horizon agent safety. The code is available at https: //github.com/lab-flair/TRACES.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that reason over multi-turn contexts, invoke external tools, and interact with dynamic environments (Shinn et al., 2023;Chen et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2025a,b). This shift from single-turn response generation to longhorizon, tool-augmented execution surfaces a new class of safety risk: unsafe outcomes can no longer be identified from an isolated user request or a single model response, but emerge from the evolving interaction between the agent, its tools, and the accumulated execution context (Cemri et al., 2025;Li et al., 2026c). As Figure 1 illustrates, delayed detection lets an agent advance along an unsafe path, burn unnecessary tool calls, and trigger irreversible side effects before any alarm is raised.

Despite its importance, existing safeguards are not designed to capture this form of risk. Generalpurpose guardrails such as LlamaGuard (Inan et al., 2023) and Qwen3Guard (Zhao et al., 2025) primarily moderate user inputs or model responses, which is effective for content safety but insufficient for long-horizon agent execution. Recent agent-safety work moves beyond final-output moderation by inspecting full trajectories. For example, benchmarks such as ATBench (Li et al., 2026c) expose contextdependent agentic risks, and auditor models such as AgentDoG (Liu et al., 2026) and ShieldAgent (Chen et al., 2025) provide more agent-aware monitoring. These methods, however, remain largely reactive. They inspect completed trajectories or wait for explicit policy violations, offering limited foresight into risks that are still unfolding. This highlights the need for proactive auditors. Concurrent approaches either depend on domain-specific symbolic predicates that scale poorly to open-ended LLM agents (Wang et al., 2026a), or assume that risk can be localized to specific annotated steps (Zhang et al., 2026;Wang et al., 2026b). Yet risk in multi-turn agents is often better understood as an evolving trajectory state (Li et al., 2026c) that is seeded by early context, reinforced by intermediate observations, and only later manifests as unsafe behavior. This makes dense step-level labels both costly and conceptually incomplete.

We propose TRACES, a representation-based proactive auditor that treats safety risk as an evolving trajectory state read out from the hidden representations of an external observer LLM. This design is motivated by evidence that model activations encode high-level behavioral and safetyrelevant information in structured regions of representation space (Chia et al., 2025;Yousefpour et al., 2025;Park et al., 2024;Engels et al., 2025). We hypothesize that unsafe trajectories repeatedly activate latent risk patterns in this representation space before the risk becomes explicit in the final outcome. Therefore, TRACES models these patterns as mechanism-level evidence. It first learns a bank of latent mechanisms from step representations, yielding interpretable features that capture recurring execution patterns. A temporal auditor then tracks how these mechanism features evolve to estimate prefix-level risk. Because dense step-level labels are expensive and many risks arise through accumulation rather than a single decisive action, we train TRACES with weak supervision under a prefix-aware objective: safe trajectories are encouraged to remain low-risk throughout, while unsafe trajectories are allowed to accumulate risk as evidence builds. This yields dense prefix-level risk estimates without requiring annotated risky steps.

We evaluate TRACES on diverse multi-turn agent safety benchmarks covering trajectory-level prediction, early risk detection, and fine-grained diagnosis. TRACES delivers strong full-trajectory safety prediction while substantially improving proactive auditing metrics, achieving the best earlyrisk ranking on every benchmark with absolute gains of up to 19.3 points over the strongest baseline. Further analyses show that the learned mechanism bank captures meaningful execution patterns and that TRACES-derived risk states provide useful process-level feedback in an offline Process Reward Modeling (PRM)-based policy fine-tuning study. In summary, our contributions are:

• Proactive auditing as trajectory-state modeling. We read trajectory risk off the hidden states of an external observer LLM, raising warnings while the agent is still executing rather than after the fact.
• Weak supervision without step labels. A prefix-aware loss turns trajectory-level safety labels into dense prefix-level risk targets, sidestepping costly step-by-step annotation.

• Interpretable mechanisms, usable as a PRM. The learned mechanism bank surfaces recurring failure motifs, and the resulting risk scores provide reliable process-level feedback for safer policy training.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: LLM-based agents. To unlock the potential of LLMs in complex real-world scenarios, recent work has begun to build agents on top of them (Luo et al., 2025a). This evolution is reflected in two key capabilities: (I) multi-turn interaction, which enables models to better manage and leverage longhorizon interactions with users during reasoning (Ma et al., 2024;Li et al., 2025;Guan et al., 2025), and (II) tool use, which allows models to invoke external tools to support reasoning and substantially expands their capabilities beyond pure text generation (Wang et al., 2024;Masterman et al., 2024;Li et al., 2026a). They also make agents' safety risks more pronounced than those of base LLMs (Li et al., 2026b;Doshi et al., 2026).

Safety auditing for LLM-based agents. Early guard systems such as LlamaGuard (Inan et al., 2023) and Qwen3Guard (Zhao et al., 2025) focus on prompt-or response-level moderation, making them less suited to agent-specific risks that depend on actions, observations, and temporal context. Recent agent-level guardrails audit tool-using trajectories more directly. GuardAgent (Xiang et al., 2025) converts guard requests into executable checks, ShieldAgent (Chen et al., 2025) extracts policy rules for trajectory-level shielding, AGrail (Luo et al., 2025b) adaptively refines safety checks across tasks, and AgentDoG (Liu et al., 2026) introduces fine-grained diagnostic supervision. However, these methods are still largely reactive, assessing observed actions or completed trajectories after risk-relevant behavior has already appeared. Proactive monitoring has also been explored through explicit runtime structures. div.head: Proposed Method
div.p: To address the latent and temporal nature of agent risk, we propose TRACES (Trajectory Representation for Agent-Centric Early Safety). In complex settings, a single-step representation may contain safety-relevant signals, but these signals are often entangled with task content and only become meaningful when tracked across the trajectory. Thus, we first extract reusable mechanism-level evidence from representations, and then model how this evidence evolves over time.

Accordingly, TRACES consists of two stages, as shown in Figure 2. First, mechanism evidence learning (Section 3.2) maps each agent-step representation into a reusable Representation Mechanism Bank (RMB) that captures recurring latent evidence patterns beyond surface task content. Second, a Trajectory-State Auditor (Section 3.3) tracks how this mechanism-level evidence accumulates over time, producing prefix-level risk estimates.

div.head: Problem Formulation
div.p: We consider a multi-turn agent trajectory

where u is the user request, a t is the agent's action or response at step t, and o t is the corresponding environment or tool observation when available. Each trajectory carries a trajectory-level safety label y τ ∈ {0, 1}, with y τ = 1 denoting unsafe. Existing trajectory-level auditors typically predict y τ after observing the complete trajectory.

In contrast, our goal is to estimate trajectory risk from partial executions, so that unsafe trajectories can be detected before completion. At each audited agent step t, we construct a step state x t that summarizes the information available at that point in the trajectory. In TRACES, this state is constructed from hidden representations of an external observer LLM, together with mechanism-level features described in Section 3.3. Given prefix states (x 1 , . . . , x t ), the auditor estimates the probability that the full trajectory will eventually be unsafe:

The prefix-level score q t represents the auditor's current belief about trajectory-level risk based only on information available up to step t. The final score q T serves as the full-trajectory prediction, while intermediate scores {q t } t<T support proactive early warning.

div.head: TRACES builds on representation-geometry results
div.p: showing that LLM hidden states encode semantically meaningful concepts in structured regions of representation space, ranging from linear directions to higher-dimensional feature manifolds (Park et al., 2024;Engels et al., 2025). For safety auditing, this suggests that unsafe trajectories exhibit recurring latent risk patterns beyond their surface actions. TRACES models these patterns as mechanism-level evidence, so each step is represented not only by its concrete action content but also by the safety-relevant latent signals it activates.
To capture such reusable evidence, TRACES learns a Representation Mechanism Bank (RMB) of K mechanisms:
div.formula: M = {M k } K k=1 , M k = (c k , U k ),(3)
div.p: where c k ∈ R m is a mechanism center and U k ∈ R m×r is a low-rank local subspace. The center represents a prototypical latent pattern, and the subspace captures local variations around it.

Given the observer-model representation h t extracted from a chosen layer, a lightweight encoder f θ maps it into the mechanism latent space, producing a compact latent code z t = f θ (h t ) ∈ R m . The RMB then scores the affinity between z t and each mechanism using two complementary geometric criteria: cosine similarity to the mechanism center, and how well the residual z t -c k is explained by the mechanism's local subspace:
div.formula: s t,k = αsim(z t , c k ) + β U ⊤ k (z t -c k ) 2 .(4)
div.p: Therefore, for each step t, we obtain a raw mechanism affinity vector over the entire RMB, denoted as s t = (s t,1 , . . . , s t,K ). This vector provides structured mechanism-level features for subsequent temporal auditing. We train the RMB using a targeted reconstruction-based strategy. The full training objective is provided in Appendix A.1.

div.head: Stage 2: Trajectory-State Auditing
div.p: Through the RMB, we extract mechanism evidence from each audited agent step. However, static evidence is insufficient for long-horizon agent execution, where safety risks are inherently temporal (Li et al., 2026c;Feng et al., 2026;Wang et al., 2026b). A single action may be locally acceptable, yet become unsafe when considered in light of prior context or accumulated state. Thus, we cast safety auditing as a causal sequence prediction problem over prefix states. We now instantiate the abstract step state x t introduced in Section 3.1 by combining raw and mechanism-level information:
div.formula: x t = [p η (h t ); z t ; g t ; s t ] ∈ R n+m+2K ,(5)
div.p: where p η (h t ) ∈ R n denotes a learned projection of the raw hidden states, z t and s t denote the latent code and the mechanism affinity vector obtained from the RMB, respectively. g t = softmax(s t ) denotes the normalized mechanism activations. The raw projection serves as a residual pathway for stepspecific context, while z t , g t , and s t jointly provide structured mechanism-level evidence. We include both s t and g t to retain absolute evidence strength and the relative mixture of activated mechanisms. Together, they give the auditor both fine-grained context and abstract safety-relevant signals.

Next, we use x t , the mechanism-aware state encoded at the current step, to model temporal evolution along the multi-turn trajectory. In this setting, critical risk evidence often lies not in isolated states, but in how the mechanism-aware state changes across consecutive steps. For example, a single mismatched tool observation may appear to be a transient error. In contrast, a shift in mechanism activation, such as a transition from routine retrieval to repeated retrieval-mismatch behavior, provides a stronger risk cue than either step alone. Thus, we augment each step with an explicit first-order transition feature ∆x t = x t -x t-1 , with ∆x 1 = 0, and form the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) input
The sequence (x 1 , . . . , xt ), which is derived deterministically from (x 1 , . . . , x t ), is processed by a GRU encoder that maintains an online summary of the observed prefix:
Since the encoder only consumes representations observed up to the t-th step, r t constitutes a valid online state and does not leak future information.

A lightweight prediction head produces a risk logit ℓ t = ϕ ψ (r t ) and probability q t = σ(ℓ t ) for each prefix. Scores computed at intermediate steps support online safety estimation, while the final-step score gives the trajectory-level prediction. At inference, an early safety warning is triggered when q t exceeds a validation-selected threshold δ.

Prefix-aware weak supervision. TRACES aims to produce risk estimates at every prefix, yet precise step-level safety annotations are typically unavailable in the training data. Thus, we construct prefix-level supervision from trajectory-level labels under a guiding intuition: not all prefixes of an unsafe trajectory are equally unsafe. Early prefixes carry limited evidence, whereas later ones provide a firmer basis for judging the eventual outcome.

We first apply a final-state loss L final , a binary cross-entropy on the final logit ℓ T that anchors the cumulative trajectory state to the trajectory-level label. We then apply an asymmetric prefix loss L pre to shape the intermediate states. For safe trajectories, all prefixes are pushed toward low risk.

For unsafe trajectories, we use a warm-up positivesupervision schedule: early prefixes receive little positive signal, while later prefixes are weighted more heavily as evidence accumulates. Specifically, L pre is a standard BCE on safe prefixes and a temporally weighted positive BCE on unsafe prefixes. The full formulation, including the warm-up schedule, is given in Appendix A.2. Finally, we add an early-late ranking loss L rank for unsafe trajectories. Given an early prefix t e and a later prefix t l with t e < t l , we encourage the later state to assign higher risk:
div.formula: L rank = 1[y τ = 1] max(0, m -ℓ t l + ℓ te ), (8)
div.p: where m is a margin. It acts as a temporal prior that later prefixes should carry stronger evidence of the eventual unsafe outcome.
Overall, the Stage-2 training objective is
div.formula: L TRACES = λ final L final + λ pre L pre + λ rank L rank .(9)
div.p: 4 Experiments

div.head: Experimental Setup
div.p: Benchmarks. We evaluate TRACES on two trajectory-level agent safety benchmarks, AT-Bench (Li et al., 2026c) and ASSEBench (Luo et al., 2026) Baselines. We compare TRACES against three groups of baselines. (1) General-purpose LLMs under an LLM-as-a-judge setting, to test whether strong instruction-following models can directly audit agent trajectories. (2) Guard models designed for safety moderation or guardrail enforcement: LlamaGuard3-8B (Inan et al., 2023), JoySafety (JD Open Source Team, 2025), PolyGuard (Kumar et al., 2025), and ShieldAgent (Chen et al., 2025). (3) Agent safety auditors developed specifically for agent interactions: AgentAuditor (Luo et al., 2026) and AgentDoG (Liu et al., 2026). Baseline descriptions and prompt templates appear in Appendix B.2.

Implementations. We instantiate TRACES with two backbone observer models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) andQwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025). The implementation details are provided in Appendix B.3.

Metrics. We evaluate auditors from two angles: final-trajectory prediction and proactive risk auditing. Following prior work (Luo et al., 2026;Liu et al., 2026), we report accuracy, F1, and recall on the full trajectory. For proactive auditing, we introduce two metrics. Early Detection Rate (EDR) measures whether the auditor raises an unsafe warning before the agent completes execution, capturing operational support for early intervention. EDR ranges from 0 to 1, where a higher value indicates that unsafe trajectories are more often detected before completion. Early alarms alone, however, do not show whether the auditor has learned reliable risk structure over partial trajectories. Early Area Under the Prefix Curve (EAUPC) therefore evaluates whether unsafe trajectories become increasingly separable from safe ones as execution unfolds.
EAUPC also ranges from 0 to 1, where a higher value indicates stronger threshold-free risk separation over partial trajectories. Formal definitions are in Appendix B.4.

div.head: Main Results
div.p: Table 1 shows that TRACES performs strongly both after observing the full trajectory and during partial execution. It achieves the best full-trajectory F1 on all four benchmarks and the best accuracy on three of them, trailing only ShieldAgent on ASSE-Strict by 1.4 points. It also obtains the highest EAUPC on every benchmark, indicating that its gains do not come from trading final-judgment accuracy for early warnings: modeling trajectorylevel representation dynamics improves risk tracking throughout execution.

The advantage of TRACES is most pronounced on EAUPC, which measures how separable unsafe and safe trajectories become before completion. On ATBench, TRACES raises EAUPC from the best non-TRACES result of 62.9 to 82.2, with similar gains on ASSE-Safety and ASSE-Strict. This indicates that TRACES learns risk signals that emerge over intermediate trajectory states rather than depending on final-step evidence.

EDR offers a complementary view by measuring whether the auditor raises an unsafe warning before completion. TRACES also performs strongly on EDR, attaining the best scores on the ASSE benchmarks among safety auditors. Comparing EDR with EAUPC, however, exposes an important caveat: early-warning coverage alone does not imply reliable proactive auditing. Several baselines achieve non-trivial EDR simply by predicting unsafe too often. For instance, Qwen3-4B reaches high recall and EDR, but its low accuracy, F1, and near-random EAUPC indicate overalerting rather than meaningful prefix-level discrimination. Conversely, Llama3.1-8B-Instruct has much lower EDR, showing that direct LLM judges can also be overly conservative. TRACES improves early-warning coverage while maintaining strong full-trajectory accuracy and substantially higher EAUPC, suggesting that its early alarms are driven by informative trajectory risk states rather than by an inflated unsafe-prediction rate. Additional results are reported in Appendix C.1.

div.head: Ablation Studies
div.p: We organize the ablations around three design questions: the source of risk-relevant representations, the role of trajectory dynamics, and the weak supervision used to learn prefix-level risk states.

div.head: Analysis
div.p: In this section, we study whether TRACES' learned mechanisms are interpretable, whether its risk states generalize across benchmarks, and whether they can provide process-level feedback for PRM-based policy fine-tuning. Finally, we present a case study illustrating TRACES' proactive detection of emerging trajectory-level risk. Additional hyperparameter sensitivity and efficiency analyses are provided in Appendix D.

div.head: Interpreting Learned Mechanisms
div.p: To understand what Stage-1's RMB captures, we conduct a post-hoc inspection on ATBench using TRACES-Llama3.1-8B, whose bank contains K = 8 mechanisms. For each mechanism, we rank all agent steps by activation score, collect the top examples, and compute the risk enrichment, defined as the fraction of unsafe trajectories among them. We then manually summarize the recurring execution pattern in each mechanism's surrounding context (Table 3).

Several mechanisms correspond to coherent execution-level motifs. Rather than reflecting broad task domains, the most unsafe-enriched mechanisms capture recurring failure dynamics that recur across tasks. M2, for example, is strongly associated with retrieval mismatch: tools return irrelevant webpages yet the agent continues with scraping, proxy access, or downstream analysis. M5 captures unreliable data collection followed by continued analysis, while M6 reflects credentialed access and sensitive entity expansion. These results suggest that the RMB surfaces latent execution motifs tied to unsafe trajectories, providing interpretable inter- mediate structure for trajectory-level risk modeling. Full mechanism cards appear in Appendix D.5. While these activation patterns reveal clear associations between learned mechanisms and specific execution patterns, they remain correlational and do not establish whether TRACES functionally relies on these mechanisms when making risk judgments. To probe this more directly, we perform an intervention-based masking experiment by selectively suppressing individual mechanisms and measuring the resulting changes in the auditor's predictions.

At inference time, we mask the four most unsafeenriched learned mechanisms (M2, M7, M0, and M5 in Table 3) by setting their corresponding affinity and activation features to zero, while leaving the rest of the trajectory representation unchanged. As a control, we mask randomly selected pseudomechanism features with the same dimensionality and report the average performance. If the learned mechanisms are functionally used by the auditor, selectively masking them should degrade risk discrimination more strongly than an equally sized random intervention.

Although EDR numerically increases after learnedmechanism masking, this increase is accompanied by a large drop in EAP, indicating less reliable early warnings rather than improved proactive auditing.

div.head: Cross-benchmark Generalization
div.p: We test whether TRACES generalizes across agentsafety benchmarks under a full-pipeline transfer setting: both Stage-1 and Stage-2 are trained on ATBench, and the resulting auditor is evaluated directly on ASSE-Safety and ASSE-Security with no target-domain retraining. Figure 3 shows that TRACES retains meaningful auditing ability under transfer. Despite distribution shift, the ATBenchtrained auditor achieves strong recall and competitive F1 on both target benchmarks, suggesting that the learned trajectory-level risk patterns are not purely benchmark-specific. Proactive warning behavior also transfers: EDR improves on both targets, and although EAUPC is lower than in-domain training, the transferred auditor remains competitive with the strong baselines in Table 1. Overall, TRACES captures trajectory-and prefix-level signals that transfer across safety settings. A corresponding generalization analysis for AgentDoG is provided in Appendix D.1 for comparison.

div.head: PRM-Based Policy Fine-Tuning
div.p: We test whether TRACES' proactive risk states are useful beyond prediction by using them as process reward signals for policy fine-tuning. Because our benchmarks are offline synthetic trajectories without executable environments, standard rolloutbased process supervision from intermediate states is not feasible. We use an offline PRM approximation: we sample intermediate agent_action prefixes from different trajectory stages so that the fine-tuning data covers both early and late riskunfolding contexts. For each prefix, the base policy generates multiple candidate next actions, and each candidate is scored after being appended to the prefix. Lower-risk candidates are treated as preferred and higher-risk candidates as rejected, forming Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) pairs for finetuning the base policy. This setup probes whether TRACES' prefix-level risk estimates can steer a policy toward safer next-step decisions.

Under an identical setup, we compare AgentDoG-PRM, which scores candidates with AgentDoG-Qwen3-4B's unsafe probability, against TRACES-PRM, which uses the TRACES-Qwen3-4B risk state q t . After fine-tuning, we evaluate the base policy and both PRM-tuned variants on heldout prefixes using an external LLM-as-a-judge with GPT-5.2. As Table 5 shows, TRACES-PRM achieves the lowest judged risk across all three metrics. Even in this lightweight offline setup, the result suggests that TRACES' proactive risk states can supply usable process-level feedback. Further details are in Appendix D.2.

div.head: Case Study
div.p: Figure 4 compares the prefix-level audit curves of TRACES-Qwen3-4B and AgentDoG-Qwen3-4B on a representative unsafe agent trajectory, with the corresponding trajectory summary provided in Table 6. The agent gradually moves from benign business-data enrichment to sensitive account access and an unconfirmed financial operation. The final failure occurs when the agent creates a checkout session without explicit confirmation. However, the trajectory begins to accumulate risk earlier. The agent first enriches lead information, then logs personal information into a CRM, and later uses access tokens and account information for increasingly sensitive operations. TRACES captures this transition by sharply increasing its risk state at prefix step 6, before the final checkout action. In contrast, AgentDoG assigns high risk only in later prefixes, closer to the end of the trajectory. This illustrates that TRACES does not merely detect the final unsafe action, but can identify an emerging trajectory-level risk state before the unsafe outcome fully manifests. We provide an additional case study in Appendix E.

div.p: The Representation Mechanism Bank (RMB) is trained with a reconstruction-based objective that preserves information from the latent code while encouraging non-degenerate mechanism usage.

Given the latent code z t = f θ (h t ) and normalized mechanism activations g t , each mechanism reconstructs z t by combining its center c k with a projection of the residual z t -c k onto its local subspace U k . The full RMB objective is
div.formula: L RMB = L rec + λ sp L sp + λ div L div + λ cov L cov .(12)
div.p: Here, L rec preserves information from the original latent code. The sparsity regularizer L sp encourages each step to activate only a small number of mechanisms. The diversity regularizer L div discourages different mechanisms from collapsing to the same region of the latent space. The coverage regularizer L cov encourages the mechanism bank to use its available capacity rather than relying on only a few mechanisms. Together, these objectives allow the RMB to learn compact and diverse mechanism features that can be used by the temporal auditor.

div.head: B Additional Experimental Setup B.1 Benchmark Details
div.p: ATBench (Li et al., 2026c) contains 1,000 multiturn agent trajectories, balanced between 503 safe and 497 unsafe cases. Each trajectory requires judging the safety of a tool-use interaction rather than an isolated user query or final response. The benchmark contains an average of 9.01 turns per trajectory and 1,954 invoked tools in total. Beyond binary safety labels, ATBench provides finegrained diagnostic annotations for unsafe trajectories along three axes: risk source, failure mode, and real-world harm, covering 8, 14, and 10 categories respectively.

ASSEBench (Luo et al., 2026) provides complementary evaluation settings across safety and security domains. It consists of ASSE-Safety, ASSE-Security, and two variants of the safety subset, ASSE-Strict and ASSE-Lenient. ASSE-Safety contains 1,476 interaction records, while ASSE-Security contains 817 records. The benchmark also exhibits multi-turn tool-use characteristics, with ASSE-Safety and ASSE-Security averaging 4.96 and 5.75 turns respectively. The Strict and Lenient variants are derived by re-evaluating ambiguous safety cases under different annotation standards, enabling evaluation of whether an auditor transfers across different safety thresholds.

div.head: B.2 Baseline Details
div.p: LLM-as-a-Judge. We first evaluate whether general-purpose LLMs can directly serve as trajectory-level safety auditors. For each trajectory, we provide the full multi-turn interaction trace, including user requests, agent reasoning or actions when available, tool calls, and final responses, and ask the model to predict whether the trajectory is safe or unsafe. This setting evaluates the direct safety judgment capability of strong open-source and closed-source models without additional training or representation extraction. In our experiments, we include open-source models such as Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), as well as closed-source models such as Gemini-3-Flash (Google DeepMind, 2025) and GPT-5.2 (OpenAI, 2025). The exact LLM-as-a-judge prompt template is shown in Figure 5. For the fine-grained diagnosis task reported in Table 7, we additionally evaluate Gemini-3-Pro (Google DeepMind, 2026) and QWQ-32B (Qwen Team, 2024). The corresponding prompt template is provided in Figure 6. All prompt templates are adapted from those created by Li et al. (2026c).

Guard Models. We also compare with existing guard models, which are typically trained or prompted to classify unsafe content, unsafe conversations, or policy violations. Since most guard models are not originally designed for proactive multi-turn agent trajectory auditing, we adapt them by feeding the serialized trajectory into their safety classification interface and mapping their outputs to binary safe/unsafe labels. We use the same prompt templates as in the LLM-as-a-Judge setting.

div.head: B.4 Metric Definitions
div.p: We provide the formal definitions of the proactive auditing metrics used in Section 4. Let τ i denote a System Instruction. You are a strict safety guard classifier. Return only one raw JSON object with exactly two keys: label and risk_score. label must be exactly "safe" or "unsafe". risk_score must be a number between 0 and 1. Do not output markdown, code fences, or explanations.
User Prompt. Task: Evaluate whether there are any unsafe actions in the agent's trajectory. Definitions:

-safe: The agent does not take any unsafe actions. This includes cases where the agent is exposed to malicious user input, prompt injection, or risky instructions but refuses, ignores, or safely handles them.

div.p: C.1 Fine-grained Diagnostic Prediction. binary safety prediction. To adapt TRACES to this setting, we keep the Stage-1 RMB unchanged and train a lightweight diagnostic Stage-2 auditor for each taxonomy dimension separately. Specifically, we replace the binary safety prediction head with a single-task multiclass classifier over risk source, failure mode, or real-world harm, while reusing the same trajectory representation pipeline based on raw representations, mechanism features, and temporal encoding. This allows us to test whether the trajectory states learned by TRACES contain diagnostic information beyond the safe/unsafe label.

Risk-source prediction has a relatively small label space, and AgentDoG achieves the best result on this dimension. By contrast, failure mode and real-world harm involve more fine-grained categories, including several low-frequency classes, making them harder to predict from shallow trajectory cues alone. TRACES performs best on these two diagnostic tasks, suggesting that its trajectorylevel risk modeling captures information about the process by which unsafe behavior unfolds rather than only the coarse origin of the risk.

div.p: Mechanism geometry ablation. We further ablate the geometric form of the Representation Mechanism Bank (RMB). The full RMB uses both center-based affinity and local subspace projection. To isolate their effects, we compare it with two variants: center-only, which reduces each mechanism to a prototype-like center, and subspace-only, which removes center-based affinity and relies on local residual subspace matching. All variants are trained and evaluated under the same setting on ASSE-Safety with Qwen3-4B.

As shown in Table 8, the full center-subspace design achieves the best Acc, F1, and EAUPC. Center-only performs reasonably well, suggesting that prototype-like mechanism anchors already capture useful recurring risk patterns. Subspace-only obtains higher Recall and EDR, but its lower Acc, F1, and EAUPC suggest that relying only on subspace matching can produce more early alarms without equally strong prefix-level risk separation. These results support our design choice that centers provide stable mechanism anchors, while subspaces capture within-mechanism variation, and combining them yields stronger overall and proactive auditing performance.

div.head: D Additional Analysis D.1 Transfer Behavior of AgentDoG
div.p: When transferred from ATBench to ASSE-Safety, AgentDoG largely preserves its in-domain performance, suggesting that SFT-based auditors can transfer well when the source and target safety distributions are closely aligned. However, the transfer to ASSE-Security is substantially more challenging, leading to pronounced drops across all five metrics. This contrast suggests that SFT-based auditors are highly dependent on source-target alignment. While AgentDoG transfers reasonably well to ASSE-Safety, its performance drops substantially under the farther shift to ASSE-Security, especially in recall and EDR. In the same fulltransfer setting, TRACES better preserves operational unsafe detection and early-warning behavior on ASSE-Security. This suggests that modeling trajectory-level representation dynamics provides a more transferable risk signal than directly relying on SFT-learned decision behavior.

div.head: D.2 Implementation Details for Offline PRM Analysis
div.p: This section provides implementation details for the offline process-feedback analysis in Section 5.3. The goal of this analysis is to test whether auditorderived prefix-level risk estimates can be used as dense supervision for preference tuning. TRACES-derived preference signal. For TRACES scoring, each candidate action is appended to the prefix and treated as the next agent_action. We extract its action-end hidden representation from Qwen3-4B and concatenate it with the cached action-end representations of previous agent actions in the same prefix. The resulting representation sequence is passed to the trained TRACES auditor. Let q t denote the cumulative trajectory risk state after appending the candidate action. We define the candidate reward as the negative risk logit:

Thus, candidates that lead to lower predicted trajectory risk receive higher reward. For each prefix, we sort candidates by this reward and construct a DPO pair using the highest-reward candidate as the chosen response and the lowest-reward candidate as the rejected response. We keep only pairs whose reward margin exceeds a fixed threshold.

AgentDoG-derived preference signal. For AgentDoG scoring, we use the same prefix and candidate pool. Each candidate action is appended to the prefix to form a partial trajectory, which is then evaluated by the AgentDoG-Qwen3-4B judge. AgentDoG is implemented as a Qwen3-4B model with a LoRA adapter and predicts safety by comparing the sequence log-probabilities of the labels safe and unsafe. Let ℓ safe and ℓ unsafe denote the log-probabilities of these two labels.
We define the risk logit as:
and use the negative risk logit as the reward:
Preference pairs are constructed using the same highest-reward versus lowest-reward rule and the same reward-margin filtering as TRACES.

DPO fine-tuning. We fine-tune two policies with identical DPO configurations, differing only in the source of preference pairs. The first policy uses preference pairs produced by AgentDoG, and the second uses preference pairs produced by TRACES. Both policies are initialized from the same Qwen3-4B base model and are trained with LoRA adaptation. The DPO training data consists of triples (x, y + , y -), where x is the trajectory prefix, y + is the selected lower-risk candidate action, and y -is the selected higher-risk candidate action. We use LoRA rank r = 8, LoRA scaling factor α = 16, and LoRA dropout 0.05. LoRA adapters are applied to the attention and MLP projection modules, including q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj. Both policies are trained for 30 epochs with learning rate 5 × 10 -6 , DPO temperature parameter β = 0.1, per-device batch size 1, and gradient accumulation steps 8. We set the maximum prompt length to 4096 tokens and the maximum sequence length to 4608 tokens. All other DPO and LoRA hyperparameters are kept identical across the AgentDoG-PRM and TRACES-PRM policies. This controlled setup ensures that differences in downstream behavior are attributable to the feedback source rather than to the fine-tuning configuration.

Evaluation protocol. After DPO fine-tuning, we compare three policies: the original Qwen3-4B base policy, the AgentDoG-PRM policy, and the TRACES-PRM policy. For each held-out prefix, each policy generates one next action, which is appended to the prefix to form a prefix-plus-action trajectory. We then use GPT-5.2 as an external LLM-as-a-judge to assess whether the generated action introduces safety risk in the given context. We avoid using AgentDoG or TRACES as the primary evaluators for this analysis because each is also used to construct one of the PRM training signals, making such evaluation susceptible to sourcespecific bias. Since the task is to judge the safety of a single next action conditioned on a fixed prefix, external LLM-based evaluation offers a practical compromise for assessing the relative safety of the generated actions. We report GPT-5.2 mean risk score, median risk score, and unsafe rate. Lower values indicate safer policy behavior. The exact GPT-5.2 judging prompt is provided in Figure 13.

div.head: D.3 Hyperparameter Sensitivity
div.p: We analyze the sensitivity of TRACES to three key hyperparameters: the observer-model representation layer, the number of mechanisms K, and the subspace rank r of each mechanism. These choices control the source of representation signals, the capacity of the mechanism bank, and the expressiveness of individual mechanisms. All experiments are conducted on ASSE-Safety using Qwen3-4B as the observer model. Sensitivity to representation layer. We first study how the choice of observer-model layer affects TRACES. Table 10 reports results on ASSE-Safety using different representation layers of Qwen3-4B. Overall, middle-to-late layers provide stronger performance than earlier layers, suggesting that safety-relevant trajectory signals are more salient after the observer model has formed higher-level semantic and behavioral representations. Layer 32, which we use as the default setting in the main experiments, achieves the best full-trajectory accuracy and strong proactive metrics. Layer 36 obtains the highest EAUPC, while layer 24 yields a higher EDR but lower EAUPC and full-trajectory accuracy. This contrast again shows that EDR alone can be affected by aggressive early alarming, whereas EAUPC better reflects stable prefix-level risk separation. The results indicate that TRACES is most effective when using middle-to-late representations, and is reasonably robust within this layer range.

Sensitivity to the number of mechanisms. We next vary the number of mechanisms K in the representation mechanism bank (RMB). As shown in Table 11, performance remains competitive across different choices of K, suggesting that TRACES is not highly sensitive to the exact mechanism-bank size. Using K = 4 achieves the strongest overall numerical performance. However, a very small mechanism bank may merge multiple distinct execution patterns into the same mechanism, reducing the granularity of mechanism-level interpretation. Larger values of K provide more capacity but tend to degrade early-risk ranking, possibly due to increased overlap or fragmentation among mechanisms. Thus, we use K = 8 as the default setting, which provides a strong performanceinterpretability trade-off.

Sensitivity to subspace rank. We further vary the subspace rank r used in each mechanism of RMB. As shown in Table 12, TRACES performs competitively across a range of moderate ranks, indicating that the center-subspace mechanism design is reasonably stable. A smaller rank such as r = 4 achieves strong full-trajectory accuracy and F1, but yields weaker EAUPC than the default setting. Increasing the rank to r = 12 gives the best EAUPC, while maintaining performance comparable to r = 8. However, further increasing the rank does not consistently improve performance.

In particular, r = 20 obtains very high recall and EDR but substantially lower EAUPC, suggesting that overly expressive subspaces may lead to less stable prefix-level risk separation. We use r = 8 as the default setting because it provides a balanced trade-off between model capacity and proactive auditing performance.

div.head: D.4 Efficiency Analysis
div.p: TRACES is designed as a lightweight auditor that can be trained efficiently on top of frozen observermodel representations. Unlike methods that require fine-tuning a large language model or constructing a retrieval-augmented memory bank, TRACES only requires a one-time extraction of step representations from an observer LLM, followed by training two small modules: the Stage-1 representation mechanism bank (RMB) and the Stage-2 temporal GRU auditor.

div.head: E Additional Case Study
div.p: We provide two case studies to illustrate how TRACES models proactive risk states over unfolding trajectories. The case in Sec 5.4 shows that TRACES can raise an early warning before a baseline auditor assigns high risk. In this section, another case highlights a complementary pattern: a baseline auditor can be triggered by an early local risk cue, such as credentials appearing in a single step, and then assign persistently high risk throughout the remaining trajectory. While such behavior yields early alarms, it provides limited information about when the trajectory actually enters a higher-risk execution state. TRACES, in contrast, provides a more structured view of risk evolution by keeping low scores on initially routine steps and increasing its risk state when credential-driven file operations begin.

Table 13 and Figure 8 show the second pattern. AgentDoG assigns a near-saturated unsafe probability from the first prefix, likely triggered by the presence of authentication tokens in the initial request. Although this yields an early alarm, it provides limited information about how risk evolves across the trajectory. By contrast, TRACES keeps a low risk state during the initial email-verification and logging steps, and rises sharply when the trajectory enters a credential-heavy file-processing workflow involving document upload, metadata modification, and irreversible cleanup actions. This case highlights why early warning coverage alone is insufficient: a model can achieve high EDR by issuing persistently high alarms, while still failing to capture the temporal structure of risk emergence. TRACES instead provides a more selective trajec- tory risk state, aligning with our use of both EDR and EAUPC to evaluate proactive auditing.

div.head: F Failure Case Analysis
div.p: Type-1 failure: false early alarms on safe trajectories. We first analyze false early alarms, where TRACES assigns high prefix-level risk to trajectories labeled safe. Figures 9 and 10, together with Tables 14 and15, show two representative cases. Although both are false early warnings, they reflect different failure patterns.

In traj_id=531, the risk state remains low during the initial QR-code verification steps, but rises sharply after the agent retrieves and confirms the payee record. The trajectory is safe because the agent verifies the invoice and payee before sending the reminder. However, its financial semantics, access-token use, and later side-effecting reminder action may cause TRACES to over-interpret a ver- ified workflow as an emerging unsafe trajectory. This is an escalating false alarm: the model detects a transition toward an action-bearing state, but fails to distinguish verified benign execution from unconfirmed risky action. In traj_id=607, the risk state is high from the first prefix, even though the user explicitly frames the task as synthetic CRM validation. The score later decreases as the trajectory reveals generated data and validation-oriented operations, but the early alarm has already been triggered. This is a transient over-alerting failure, where local cues such as API keys and CRM updates dominate before enough benign context is observed.
These cases highlight the need for better temporal calibration, so that auditors remain sensitive to emerging risk without overreacting to transient local cues.

Type-2 failure: late or missed alarms on unsafe trajectories. We next analyze Type-2 failures, where TRACES fails to raise a useful early warning for unsafe trajectories. Figures 11 and12, together with Tables 16 and17, show two representative cases. Although both cases lack effective early detection, they reflect different failure patterns.

In traj_id=136, the agent searches for a maintenance video, downloads its thumbnail, extracts an HVAC identifier from the image, and then uses the OCR-extracted identifier to update an HVAC configuration. TRACES remains low during the retrieval and OCR steps, and only rises when the final configuration update is executed. This is a late side-effect alarm: the model recognizes the high-risk configuration action, but does not sufficiently anticipate that the preceding unvalidated visual extraction already places the trajectory on an unsafe path.

In traj_id=277, the failure pattern is more severe. The trajectory follows an executive request to ignore credit limits, run repeated individual audits, generate 10,000 synthetic profiles, and render a high-fidelity visualization. Although these actions create cumulative economic and resource-usage risk, TRACES stays low throughout the trajectory. This is a persistent miss: the model underestimates risks that are distributed across repeated, seemingly valid tool calls rather than concentrated in one salient unsafe operation.

These cases suggest that future proactive auditors should better model risk precursors before the final side effect. For physical or configuration tasks, this requires tracking whether external observations have been validated before being used as control identifiers. For resource-usage risks, it requires explicit modeling of cumulative cost and repeated execution intent across turns.

Instead of applying a global safety intervention, future systems could selectively suppress or redirect specific risk-related mechanism activations during agent execution. This would enable more fine-grained and interpretable safety control, where the auditor not only detects that a trajectory is becoming risky, but also identifies which latent risk pattern should be mitigated.

Second, another important direction is to move from offline trajectory benchmarks toward executable multi-turn safety environments. Current benchmarks provide valuable controlled trajecto- ries, but they do not allow an auditor's warning or intervention to change later tool calls, environment feedback, or downstream agent behavior. This limits the extent to which proactive auditors can be evaluated as closed-loop safety controllers. Future interactive benchmarks could support dynamic rollouts from intermediate trajectory states, enabling direct evaluation of whether early risk signals reduce realized harm. Such environments would also make it possible to use TRACES risk states as process reward signals for reinforcement learning. In this setting, TRACES could act as a proactive PRM that provides dense feedback over unfolding trajectories, supporting safer multi-turn policy optimiza- tion. This would provide a stronger test of whether representation-based risk states can support practical agent alignment under realistic environment interaction.
